questions.stem: A 120 V source is connected across a 24 ohm resistive load. What current flows through the load?
options: 0.20 A (amperes)
2.88 A (amperes)
5.0 A (amperes)
2,880 A (amperes)
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Using Ohm’s law, I = V / R = 120 V / 24 ohms = 5.0 A (amperes).
incorrectOptionExplanations: This reverses the relationship or divides resistance by voltage.
This value does not result from the voltage-to-resistance ratio.
This result is three orders of magnitude too large for the stated values.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, Ohm's law and electrical calculations, pp. 427-432

questions.stem: A single-phase resistive load operates at 480 V and draws 30 A. What electrical power is delivered?
options: 144 kW
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For the stated resistive single-phase calculation, P = V × I = 480 × 30 = 14,400 W = 14.4 kW.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This result is low by a factor of ten.
Dividing voltage by current does not calculate power.
This result is high by a factor of ten.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, electrical power calculations, pp. 429-432

questions.stem: A 1.5 kW device operates 8 hours per day for 20 days. Electricity costs $0.12 per kWh. What is the operating energy cost?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Energy = 1.5 kW × 8 h/day × 20 days = 240 kWh. Cost = 240 × $0.12 = $28.80.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This omits half of the required operating time or cost.
This is five times the correct cost and does not follow the stated rate.
This shifts the decimal one place and overstates the cost by a factor of ten.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, power and energy calculations, pp. 429-432

questions.stem: Three resistors of 12 ohms, 18 ohms, and 30 ohms are connected in series. What is total resistance?
options: 6 ohms
60 ohms
20 ohms
6480 ohms
incorrectOptionExplanations: Six ohms is below every listed resistance and cannot be the sum of series components.
Twenty ohms is the arithmetic mean, not the series total.
Multiplying all three resistances is not the formula for a series circuit.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, series circuits and resistance, pp. 428-433

questions.stem: Two resistors of 120 ohms and 240 ohms are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
options: 120 ohms
180 ohms
80 ohms
360 ohms
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For two parallel resistors, R = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2) = (120 × 240) / 360 = 80 ohms.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Equivalent parallel resistance must be less than the smallest branch resistance.
Averaging the two values does not calculate parallel resistance.
Adding the resistances gives a series result, not a parallel result.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, parallel circuits and resistance, pp. 428-433

questions.stem: Two workers contact energized equipment under different conditions. Which factors most directly determine the severity of electrical shock injury?
options: The conductor color, equipment purchase date, and manufacturer logo.
Only the source voltage, regardless of body resistance or contact duration.
Only whether the worker is standing or sitting when contact occurs.
Current magnitude, path through the body, contact duration, and current frequency.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Shock severity depends on the current that actually passes through the body, its path, how long it flows, and electrical characteristics. Voltage affects current but is not the sole determinant.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Administrative product details do not determine the physiological effect of current through the body.
Voltage is important, but current depends on the complete contact conditions and injury also depends on path and duration.
Body position may influence circumstances but is not the complete set of controlling electrical-injury factors.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, electrical shock hazard and current effects, pp. 436-438

questions.stem: A portable tool develops leakage current through a worker toward ground. What protective action is a GFCI designed to take?
options: Detect unequal outgoing and returning current and rapidly interrupt the circuit.
Increase the branch-circuit breaker rating so the tool can continue operating.
Measure conductor temperature and trip only after insulation begins to melt.
Reduce the supply frequency while leaving the leakage path energized.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A GFCI compares current in the circuit conductors. A difference indicates current is escaping through another path, potentially a person, so the device opens the circuit quickly.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Increasing overcurrent protection would worsen the hazard and is not the operating principle of a GFCI.
A GFCI responds to current imbalance rather than waiting for thermal damage.
Changing frequency is not the protective mechanism and would not remove the ground-fault path.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.304 - Wiring Design and Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, ground-fault circuit interrupters, pp. 440-441; OSHA 1910.304(b)(3)

questions.stem: A worker removes the grounding pin from a three-prong tool plug so it will fit a two-slot receptacle. Why is this unsafe?
options: It causes the tool motor to run at exactly half its designed speed.
It removes the intended fault-current path, allowing an exposed metal frame to remain energized.
It converts alternating current to direct current inside the tool housing.
It increases the insulation resistance and prevents the branch breaker from sensing normal load current.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The equipment grounding conductor provides a fault-current path that helps protective devices operate and limits dangerous voltage on exposed metal. Removing the pin defeats that protection.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Grounding-pin removal does not intentionally control motor speed.
The grounding connection does not convert the type of electrical current.
Removing the ground does not increase protective insulation; it removes a critical fault path.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.334 - Use of Equipment
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, improper grounding, pp. 440-441; OSHA 1910.334(a)(3)

questions.stem: A high-current tool is connected through an undersized extension cord to a branch circuit whose breaker is sized for the building wiring. Why can the cord overheat without an immediate breaker trip?
options: Extension cords cannot produce heat because flexible insulation removes electrical resistance.
The branch breaker responds only to voltage and cannot detect any current condition.
The cord can exceed its ampacity while current stays below the branch-breaker trip level.
The grounding conductor carries the entire normal load, preventing the breaker from measuring it.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Overcurrent protection must be coordinated with conductor ampacity. A smaller extension-cord conductor can be overloaded by current that is still below the branch breaker’s trip threshold.
incorrectOptionExplanations: All conductors have resistance and can heat when current exceeds their safe carrying capacity.
Circuit breakers respond to overcurrent, but their rating may not protect a smaller downstream cord.
The normal load flows through the current-carrying conductors, not entirely through the grounding conductor.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.304 - Wiring Design and Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, inadequate wiring and overloaded circuits, pp. 439-442; OSHA 1910.304(f)(1)(i)

questions.stem: Before a shift, an employee finds a crushed extension-cord jacket and a loose grounding pin. What should happen next?
options: Wrap the damaged area with ordinary tape and use the cord only for low-power tools.
Continue using it if the circuit is protected by a standard thermal-magnetic breaker.
Cut off the grounding pin so the plug can be inserted more easily and inspect it next month.
Remove the cord from service until repairs and tests necessary to make it safe have been completed.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Cord sets must be visually inspected before use when applicable. A defect that could expose an employee to injury requires removal from service until the item has been properly repaired and tested.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Ordinary tape does not restore the cord’s approved construction or correct a loose grounding connection.
A branch breaker does not make damaged insulation or grounding hardware safe for use.
Removing a grounding pin further defeats protection and does not correct the damaged cord.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.334 - Use of Equipment
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, defective or damaged cords, pp. 439-440; OSHA 1910.334(a)(2)

questions.stem: A mechanic presses a machine stop button and assumes the electrical cabinet is safe to open. What additional actions are required before treating circuit parts as deenergized?
options: Isolate sources, apply lockout/tagout, control stored energy, and verify absence of voltage with proper test equipment.
Rely on the stop button because control-circuit devices are accepted as the sole energy-isolation method.
Open the cabinet immediately if the indicator lamp is dark and the motor is no longer moving.
Ask another employee to watch the start button while the mechanic contacts the circuit parts.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Push buttons and interlocks are not energy-isolating devices. The electrical source must be disconnected, locked and tagged, stored energy addressed, and the deenergized condition verified before work.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Control-circuit devices can fail or be bypassed and cannot serve as the sole means of deenergizing.
A stopped motor or dark indicator does not prove that every source and circuit part is deenergized.
Administrative observation of a start control does not isolate energy or verify absence of voltage.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.333 - Selection and Use of Work Practices
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, electrical lockout/tagout and work practices, pp. 442-450; OSHA 1910.333(b)(2)

questions.stem: Troubleshooting requires measurements on exposed energized parts because deenergizing would make the diagnostic test impossible. Who may perform the work?
options: Any experienced production operator if a supervisor verbally authorizes the task.
A qualified person using electrical PPE, insulated tools, and required energized-work precautions.
An unqualified employee wearing leather gloves and standing on dry cardboard.
Any employee who has previously watched the same troubleshooting task being performed.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: When energized work is justified, OSHA limits it to qualified persons familiar with safe techniques and the proper use of PPE, shielding, insulating materials, and insulated tools.
incorrectOptionExplanations: General experience and verbal permission do not establish the electrical knowledge and training of a qualified person.
Leather gloves and improvised dry material are not a substitute for qualified status and appropriately rated protective equipment.
Observation alone does not demonstrate the required skills, knowledge, and safety training.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.333 and 1910.335
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, electrical safety-related work practices and PPE, pp. 442-450; OSHA 1910.333(c)(2) and 1910.335(a)

questions.stem: A technician is preparing to measure voltage in an industrial panel. Which test-equipment practice is required?
options: Use any meter that displays a voltage range above zero, regardless of its category or lead condition.
Hold damaged probe insulation away from the panel and continue if the display appears stable.
Use correctly rated, undamaged test equipment, and have a qualified person perform the voltage measurement.
Use a noncontact detector as the only proof that every conductor is deenergized before contact work.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA requires qualified persons for testing, visual inspection of instruments and leads, and ratings suitable for the circuits, equipment, and environment where they are used.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A numerical range alone does not establish the required circuit rating, environmental suitability, or safe condition.
Damaged test equipment must be removed from service rather than managed by hand position.
A noncontact indication can support screening but is not a complete substitute for an appropriately rated contact test and required verification procedure.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.334 - Use of Equipment
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, test instruments and equipment, p. 447; OSHA 1910.334(c)

questions.stem: Boxes of supplies are stored in front of a panelboard that may require energized examination. What is the appropriate correction?
options: Leave the boxes if employees can move them within five minutes after an electrical incident.
Mark the boxes with a high-voltage label and continue using the area for storage.
Stack the boxes higher so the floor area immediately in front of the panel remains partly visible.
Remove the storage and maintain the required clear access and working space around the panelboard.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Required electrical working space must be maintained for ready and safe operation and maintenance and may not be used for storage.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Working space must be continuously available; delayed removal after an event defeats its purpose.
Warning labels do not convert prohibited storage into a compliant working space.
Partial visibility does not provide the clear width, depth, access, and door-opening space required.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.303 - General Electrical Requirements
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, controlling electrical hazards, pp. 438-450; OSHA 1910.303(g)(1)

questions.concept: Arc flash and arc blast consequences
questions.stem: A fault produces a high-energy electrical arc inside switchgear. Which combination of hazards should the risk assessment consider?
options: Intense thermal energy and light, a pressure wave, and projected molten metal or equipment fragments.
Only electric shock through direct contact, because an arc cannot injure a person at a distance.
Only hearing damage, because protective clothing eliminates every thermal and pressure hazard.
Only smoke inhalation after the equipment cools, because the arc itself lasts too briefly to cause injury.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: An electrical arc can release extreme heat and light, generate a blast-pressure wave, and propel molten metal and fragments. These hazards exist in addition to possible shock.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Arc energy can cause severe injury without direct electrical contact.
Protective clothing reduces selected thermal exposure but does not eliminate blast, sound, fragment, or all burn hazards.
Very short arc duration can still release enough energy to cause immediate burns, pressure injuries, and flying debris.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.335 - Safeguards for Personnel Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, arc blasts and arc-flash risk assessment, pp. 438 and 448-450; OSHA 1910.335(a)

questions.concept: Electrical equipment in hazardous classified locations
questions.stem: A portable general-purpose fan is proposed for an area where flammable solvent vapor may be present during normal operations. What is the best decision?
options: Use the general-purpose fan if its motor is less than one horsepower and the cord is grounded.
Use electrical equipment and wiring approved or otherwise suitable for the specific hazardous location.
Use the fan only at night because lower occupancy changes the electrical area classification.
Use any fan with a metal guard because the guard prevents internal sparks from igniting vapor.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Electrical equipment in hazardous classified locations must be suitable for the class or zone and the ignitable properties of the gas, vapor, dust, or fiber present. General-purpose construction is not enough.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Motor size and grounding do not establish approval for a flammable-vapor hazardous location.
Area classification depends on material properties and likelihood of a hazardous concentration, not the time of day or occupancy alone.
A metal guard does not prevent internal arcing, hot surfaces, or other ignition sources from affecting the atmosphere.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.307 - Hazardous Classified Locations
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 16, electrical hazards and equipment suitability, pp. 438-450; OSHA 1910.307(a)-(c)
